restatements.text: Prohibits landlords from raising rent by more than 5 percent in any 12-month period, except for units that were first occupied within the past 15 years.

findings.quote: A landlord of a residential unit may not increase rent by more than 5 percent in any 12-month period. This section does not apply to units first occupied within the last 15 years.
findings.mechanism: Protects renters in units older than 15 years from annual rent increases greater than 5%.

analysis.answer: Current law allows landlords to raise rent by any amount given 60 days' written notice. The measure restricts rent increases to no more than 5% in any 12-month period, exempting units that were first occupied within the last 15 years.
Renters in non-exempt units benefit from predictable, legally capped rent increases. Landlords of these units bear the cost of limited revenue potential.

Landlords of covered units may respond by raising rent by the maximum 5% every year rather than waiting and making larger, less frequent increases, to avoid permanently losing the capacity to raise rates. Some landlords may also reduce investments in maintenance or upgrades since they cannot readily recoup those costs through higher rents.

The measure addresses the problem of sudden, unmanageable rent increases that can displace existing tenants. The 5% cap directly reaches this by prohibiting such spikes for older units, while the 15-year rolling exemption attempts to avoid deterring new housing construction.

Researchers disagree on the net outcomes of rent control. Studies consistently show that rent caps benefit current tenants by keeping them in their homes and lowering their immediate housing costs. However, many economists find that rent controls eventually reduce the overall supply and quality of rental housing, which can drive up costs for future renters or those moving into uncontrolled units.
